ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
MR.   DEPUTY   CHAIRMAN:   Qu estion   Hour.   Q.No.   261, 
Shri Janardhana Poojari. 
Undesirable channels on D.T.H. Television 
*261. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJAR Y: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that it has become possible for the DTH Television 
users to view certain undesirable channels using certain types of smart 
cards; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) how this misuse of the system is proposed to be curtailed? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING AND 
CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (c) AStatement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) DTH broadcasting service refers to distribution of multichannel 
TV programmes in Ku band by using a satellite system by providing TV 
signals direct to subscribers' premises. All the distribution platforms such as 
DTH, cable networks, internet, cell phones, etc. are susceptible to misuse 
through various technical devices, including smart cards. However, the 
possibility of receiving pornographic channels through DTH service was looked 
into. The records of the private DTH Service Provider were examined by a 
am of this Ministry. It was found that the bouquet of TV channels provided 
the Service Provider did not contain any pornographic channel. 
The existing DTH license conditions for setting up and operating DTH 
Service in India contain adequate safeguards with regard to the carriage of 
1

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2004] 
undesirable contents in DTH service. The terms and conditions of the Licence 
Agreement, inter alia, make it obligatory on the part of the DTH licensee to 
adhere to the Programme and Advertisement Codes, as laid down by this 
Ministry. The use of DTH service for anti-national activities would be construed as 
an offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code and applicable laws and will 
attract immediate termination of license. 
While this Ministry is in the process of strengthening the monitoring 
arrangements in this regard, it is also contemplating a legislation to put in place a 
regulatory structure for broadcasting.

Statement 
(a) to (e) In furtherance of the Constitutional provisions, two Acts of

Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities)

Act, 1989 provide the framework for prev ention of atrocities, legal aid, 
special Courts and monitoring at all levels. The Acts also provide for laying 
Annual Reports on the measures taken by the State Governments and 
Government of India in pursuance of the provisions of the Acts. Special 
Cells are functioning in 19 States/Union Territory and exclusive Special 
Courts are also functioning in 9 States. 
The National Commissions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
also investigate and monitor all matters relating to the Constitutional 
safeguards and also evaluate their working. 
Under the Centrally Sponsored Sc heme for implementation of the 
Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, due Central 
assistance is provided to State Governments and Union Territory 
Administrations mainly for strengthening of the administrative, enforcement 
and judicial machinery, awareness generation, and relief and rehabilitation 
of the affected persons.

with these instructions.

of the 1974 directions.

Explosives in imported metal scrap 
*268.    SHRI LALIT .SURI: 
SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the countries from where metal scrap was allowed to be imported 
during 2004; 
(b) whether the imported metal scrap contained explosive war-heads both 
used and live that caused loss of life and property as live war-heads exploded 
at various places in the country; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the action taken/proposed to be taken to ensure that such dangerous 
imports are banned? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) to (d) Recently certain cases have come to the notice of the 
Government wherein metallic scrap containing used and live shells have been 
imported thereby causing explosions and consequently loss of life and 
property. These imports are clearly in violation of the Foreign Trade Policy 
and the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992. After a 
series of Inter-Ministerial consultations the Government has laid down 
certain new guidelines and procedures for import of metallic scrap and 
waste. According to these procedures import of all kinds of metallic scrap 
and waste in unshredded, compressed or loose form will be accompanied 
by a pre-inspection certificate to the effect that the imported consignment 
does not contain any ammunition, or other explosive material or radio-
active material irrespective of the source of such imports. Such imports will 
also be subject to stringent examination according to the procedures laid 
down by the Customs. Imports will also be restricted through fifteen ports 
only. 
The details of the country from where metal scrap was imported during 2004 
is available in the Publication 'Monthly Statistics of Foreign Trade of India, Vol. II 
(Imports) —Annual Number* published by Directorate General of Commercial 
intelligence & Statistics which is available in the Parliament Library.

Agreement with Gulf Co-operation Council 
*269. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) have signed a 
framework agreement on economic cooperation to give fillip to the existing 
commerical and economic ties between the two countries; 
(b) if so, whether his Ministry and the Foreign Minister of Kuwait, who is 
the Chairman of the GCC, signed an agreement in this regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) to what extent India and Gulf Cooperation Council have started 
implementing this agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) 
have signed a Framework Agreement on Economic Cooperation (FAC). 
The Agreement was jointly signed by the Minister of Commerce and Industry, 
the Foreign Minister of Kuwait, in his capacity of President of GCC and 
Secretary-General of GCC on the 25th August, 2004 in New Delhi. The 
Agreement aims at expansion and liberalisation of trade and enhancement 
of the level of economic cooperation between India and the GCC. 
(d) As a follow-up of the signing of the Agreement, research institutions 
have been entrusted with conducting studies on various aspects of the 
Framework Agreement on Economic Cooperation (FAC). Discussions were 
held with a GCC delegation in New Delhi on 19th November, 2004, in 
which both sides inter alia agreed to continue the process of dialogue in 
the context of the provisions of the Agreement.

in Europe, was successfully challenged. The claims of the patent on

Duty on import of agricultural items 
1778.. SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the agricultural items, on which import duty has been 
reduced; 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2004] 
(b) whether this reduction of impor t duty is extended only to some 
countries; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the impact of such imports on domestic market and farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.VK.S. ELANGOVAN):  (a) to (d) General rates of 
customs duty on agricultural items have not been reduced in the Budget 
for the year 2004-05. In fact, import duty on palm oils (other than crude 
palm oil) has been increased from 70 per cent to 75 per cent. 
However, as per commitments under the Early Harvest Scheme (EHS) 
of the Framework Agreement for Establishing a Free Trade Area between 
India and Thailand, customs duty on imports of certain agricultural items 
from Thailand, such as, fresh mangosteens, mangoes, fresh grapes, apples, 
durians, fresh rambutans, longans, pomegranates, and durum wheat has 
been reduced with effect from 1st September, 2004 by 50 per cent of the 
general rate of customs duty applicable on these items as on 1 st April, 2004. 
In respect of the India-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement, which was 
signed on 28th December, 1998, the implementation of preferential margins 
began in March, 2000. Under this Agreement, all agricultural products 
originating in Sri Lanka, except tea, which is importable under a Tariff Rate 
Quota regime, as well as those designated in a negative list of imports, 
are importable at zero duty with effect from 18th March, 2003. 
The Agreement on South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA), which was 
signed by Bangladesh, Bhutan, Indi a, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and 
Sri Lanka on 6th January, 2004, will come into operation from 1 st January, 
2006. However under the SAARC Preferential Trade Agreement (SAPTA) 
preferential imports into India came into operation as from 1st March, 
1997. 
India also has bilateral trade treaties with Nepal and Bhutan under which 
dutyfree imports are allowed on certain agricultural products on the principle 
of non-reciprocity from these two countries. India has also granted a margin 
of preferences of 50 per cent of the general rate of customs duty applicable 
on a limited number of fresh and dried fruit with effect from 13th May, 2003 
to imports originating in Afghanistan under the India-Afghanistan Preferential 
Trade Agreement. 
68 
 

[20 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Under the Global System of Trade Preferences (GSTP) India is granting 
preferential access to six agricultural products to constituent developing 
Member countries. Under the Bangkok Agreement preferential access is 
currently granted to nine agricultural products. 
The regional trade arrangements provide for trade defence measures 
which can be resorted to in case of a surge in imports and injury to the 
domestic industry and farmers. Moreover, the arrangements also 
incorporate cooperation among the customs authorities of the Member 
countries in order to ensure that the qualifying origin criteria are not violated. 
In specific instances, monitoring mechanisms to prevent circumvention of 
the qualifying origin criteria have also been established, such as under the 
India-Sri Lanka Free TradeAgreement.

1804. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

country, the deficit of women in population was 3 million in 1991 and 36 
million now; and

implement laws against sex determination and dowry and also to protect 
the girl child from discrimination? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) The sex ratio in the country 
was 927 females per thousand males as per the Census, 1991. The absolute 
numbers were: 403 million females compared to 435 million males. 
According to Census, 2001, the sex ratio has gone up to 933 females per 
thousand males. The absolute numbers being: 496 million females 
compared to 532 million males. 
(b) The Government has adopted the National Policy for the 
Empowerment of Women, 2001 which envisages strict enforcement of 
laws against pre-natal sex selection and elimination of all forms of 
discrimination against the girl child and violation of her rights by undertaking 
strong measures, both preventive and punitive within and outside the family. 
The Policy also lays emphasis on creating and strengtheing institutions, 
mechanisms and suitable schemes for assistance for preventing violence 
against women, including violence arising out of customs like dowry.

Education for All Global Monitoring Report by UNESCO 
1819. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the latest Education for All Global Monitoring Report by 
UNESCO; India has been placed among the groups which is very far away 
from achieving the goals for ensuring that every child goes to school by 
2015; 
(b) if so, the reasons for such dampening report vis-a-vis progress under 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan aiming the goal; and 
(c) the steps proposed to achieve Universal primary education by 2015 
in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) India has been placed among the 
countries having low Education Development Index (EDI) in the latest 
Education for All Global Monitoring Report by UNESCO. In this Report the 
EDI of India is based on educational data supplied as on 30th September 
2001. Therefore, the impact of the initiatives taken by the Government 
during the recent years under schemes like Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan are 
yet to be factored into this report. 
(c) The following steps have been taken by the Government to achieve 
Universal Elementary education by 2015 in the country:— 
(i) The foremost amongst them is the amendment of the Constitution 
through the Constitution of India (86th Amendment) Act, 2002, 
through which free and compulsory education has become a 
Fundamental Right for children in the age group 6-14 years. 
(ii) In addition, the following schemes are being implemented to provide 
education facilities to all children in the 6-14 age group including 
out of school children & dropouts in all States/UTs: 
— Sarva Siksha Abhiyan (SSA): Th is scheme aims at providing 
useful and relevant elementary education for all children in the 6 
to 14 age group by 2010 as well as to bridge social, regional and 
gender gaps, with the active participation of the community in the 
management of schools. Interventions for early childhood care 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2004] 
and education, recruitment of female teachers, provision of free 
textbooks to girls, opening and upgradation of schools to improve 
access to education, involvement of women through a participatory 
process in the effective management of schools and, 'the Mahila 
Samakhya type' of interventions that help attain the objective of 
gender parity. The National Programme for Education of Girls at 
the Elementary Level (NPEGEL) and the Kasturba Gandhi Balika 
Vidhyalaya (KGBV) are being implemented as part of the SSA to 
promote universalisation of el ementary education among girls 
belonging to the disadvantaged sections of society. 
— The Education Guarantee Schem e and Alternative & Innovative 
Education: This scheme was launched from the 1st April 2001 to 
provide access to school-less habitations. The scheme also 
supports flexible strategies for out of school children including 
bridge courses, residential ca mps, 'drop in' centers, summer 
camps and remedial coaching. 
— Mid-Day-Meal Scheme: The sche me was initially launched in 
1995-96 with the objective of providing a boost to the efforts of 
universalisation of primary education by increasing enrolment and 
retention by reducing dropouts and simultaneously impacting on 
the nutrition levels of students in primary classes. 
— The National Literacy Mission (NLM) was set up in 1988 to impart 
functional literacy to non-literates in the age group of 15-35 years 
in a time bound manner. The aim of the NLM is to achieve a 
sustainable threshold level of 75% literacy by 2007.

Biased information by TV channels and newspapers 
1840. SHRI C. PERUMAL Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some TV channels and newspapers do not give 
correct information about certain events or give biased information; and

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) and (b) Press in India is free from Government control. The Press 
Council of India (PCI) is a statutor y body established for preserving the 
freedom of the Press and for maintaining and improving the standards of 
newspapers and news agencies in India. PCI has set the Norms for Journalistic 
Ethics. Norms laid down by PCI state that Editors must check the authenticity of 
each story and comments/versions of all concerned parties must be included. 
The PCI may warn admonish or censure the newspapers, the news agency, 
the editor or the journalist or disapprove the conduct of the Editor or the journalist 
as the case may be, for offending the standards of journalistic ethics or public 
taste or for professional misconduct. 
As regards Prasar Bharati, the Prasar Bharati Charter and the 
Parthasarathy Guidelines are being strictly followed by Doordarshan News to carry 
fair and objective news. The reporting of News in Doordarshan is factual, 
accurate and objective.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Law Commission of

Judges of the Supreme Court.

Corruption in Judiciary 
†1855. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there has been rampant corruption in the 
judicial system; 
(b) if not, the Government's reaction thereto and whether it is also a fact 
that the Prime Minister has recently stated the necessity of making the 
judicial system corruption free; 
(c) if so, whether Government have decided to take some specific steps 
in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) to (d) Allegations of deviant behaviour 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
152 

[20 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
involving acts of corruption and moral turpitude against some Judges of 
High Courts and some members of Judicial Service of the States have 
come to the notice of the Government. 
Hon'ble Prime Minister, in his address to the conference of Chief Justices 
and Chief Ministers held on September 18, 2004 has inter-alia observed 
as follows: 
"The framers of our Constitution wanted to protect and preserve the 
independence of our judiciary. This places a greater onus and responsibility 
on the members and practitioners of our judiciary to maintain the highest 
standards of probity and integrity. Accountability and transparency norms 
cannot, and should not, be imposed on the judiciary from outside. It is, I 
believe, up to the judiciary to do some soul-searching and ensure how this 
can best be done." 
The Chief Justice of a High Court has the competence to receive and 
look into complaints against the conduct of a Judge of his Court. In some 
recent cases, the Chief Justice of India set up inquiry committees under 
in-house procedure to deal with cases of deviant behaviour of Judges. As 
regards the members of Judicial Service of a State, under article 235 of the 
constitution of India, the administrative control over the members of 
subordinate judiciary in the States vests with the concerned High Court 
and the State Government. Therefore, the disciplinary control in respect of 
judicial officers of subordinate judiciary lies with the concerned High Court 
and the State Government.

in-law, daughter-in-law or sister-in-law.

tribunal in which above mentioned relation of the Advocate is a

ary action against advocates vest in either the State Bar Council or the

(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) and (b) Free legal services are extended 
to the weaker sections of the society such as, Scheduled Caste, Scheduled 
Tribe, women, children handicapped, disabled workmen and persons in 
custody, under the provisions of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) and (b) The Election Commission has informed that

electoral rolls, it may be stated that the electoral rolls are maintained in

Concern over the ban imposed on religious freedom of Sikhs 
in France 
SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA(Jharkhand): Sir, the UN General Assembly on 
25th November, 1981 made a declaration for elimination of all forms of 
religious intolerance and discriminations. There are several international laws 
and conventions recognising the right to freedom of thought, conscience and 
religion. Article 18 of the Universal Decl aration of Human Rights; Article 18 of 
the International Covenant on Civil an d Political Rights; Article 9 of the 
European Convention; etc. uphold the right of a person to manifest his religion 
of belief in teaching, practices, worship and observance. Vide an amendment 
to the Code of Education in the law on secularity and conspicuous religious 
symbols in schools, France nas imposed ban on wearing of turban by Sikh 
students in public schools. This is denial of religious freedom to the Sikhs who 
constitute a miniscule minority of French population. Unshorn-hair, turban etc. 
are integral parts and inalienable element s of Sikhism. This law is seen as 
sign of religious intolerance and racial  discrimination, which is distinctly 
opposed to Indian

benevolent and non-discriminatory regi me. This is unexpected from French 
people who enjoy reputation as progressive among Europeans. Other 
European countries comprise of sizeable citizen belonging to Sikh religion and 
this ban may encourage these countries also to imitate. I apprehend this ban 
on the Sikhs may be a design to force them to either give up their religion or 
face hardships. In view of the tradition of cordial relationship between India and 
France, the House may direct the Government to urge upon French 
Government to reconsider the new law in order that the religious freedom is 
restored to their citizens belonging to Sikh religion.

SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura): Sir, there is a proverb "Justice delayed

Demand for the Development of Tourism in the country 
SHRI B.J. PANDA (Orissa): Sir, my S pecial Mention is with regard to the 
need for certain specific steps for the development of tourism. The importance 
of tourism for creating gainful employment and improving our economy cannot 
be over-emphasized. In the days to come, more jobs will

get created in the service sector, and tourism will be a leading light, which needs to 
be nurtured and developed. The basic problem with tourism today is the lack of 
infrastructure, and without making a short-term and long-term plans for 
infrastructure development, it will not be possible to translate the success of our 
recent campaign "Incredible India" into a ground reality. For this, two basic issues 
will have to be tackled. The first is, access to our country. At present, no one 
wishing to visit India on short notice, can find seats to fly as the number of seats

Singapore is attributed to the strength of their National Carriers and development of 
their own aviation sector, which should be emulated here. Another immediate task 
is to add hotel rooms. Even a small growth in traffic puts our infrastructure under 
stress. This needs to be tackled at the first opportunity. The shortage is acute in 
cities like Bangalore, Hyderabad, and even in Delhi and Mumbai. There is also a 
need to build "Budget Hotels" in India. The present policy of building of five star 
properties may be suited to the affluent visitors, but not to the tourist of average 
means. To attract more tourists, affordable budget hotels will have to be 
encouraged, and for that, the Land Development authorities should held in the 
allotment of lands at affordable prices for the specific purpose of building such 
budget hotels. Thank you.

Demand for early completion of Tuirial Hydro Electric Project in 
Mizoram and payment of compensation to the oustees on 
priority basis 
SHRI LALHMING LIANA (Mizoram): Sir, my Special Mention is regarding the 
early completion of the Tuirial Hydro Electric Project in Mizoram. 
Sir, the 60 megawatt Tuirial Hydro Electric Project (THEP) in Mizoram has 
been undertaken by the North Eastern Electric Power Corporation (NEEPCO) 
which is the only Central hydro electric power project in Mizoram. Twelve per 
cent of the power generated by THEP will be given to Mizoram free of cost and the 
rest will be distributed among the other North Eastern States. The major civil 
works had commenced in September, 2001 and over Rs. 200 crores have 
already been invested in the project. Like other projects, this project too has 
affected more than 400 families who have lost their land and means of livelihood. 
Those people have formed an association, namely, the Tuirial Compensation 
Claimant Association (TCCA). After a tripartite meeting the NEEPCO agreed to 
pay the TCCA an amount of Rs. 8.04 crores as crop compensation. The 
NEEPCO then contended that the crop compensation was illegal and the amount 
agreed at the tripartite meeting had to be treated as land compensation and thus 
refused to pay the agreed crop compensation. In protest against this 
development, the affected villagers called for a bandh on 6th June, 2004 which 
was completely peaceful. The affected people are members of tribal and minority 
communities and there is widespread unrest among them. In the meanwhile, the 
NEEPCO has stopped the construction of the project on the plea of law and order 
problems and it wants to abandon the project on false pretexts.

matter and ensure that:— 
(a) the NEEPCO pays the agreed crop compensation and land 
compensation separately; 
(b) the THEP is completed at the earliest so that the generation Of power 
starts at the earliest which will benefit Mizoram and the entire North 
East. 
Thank you.

SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI (Gujarat): Sir, Methane farming and biodiesel are the 
new renewable sources to meet our entire energy needs. Why should we import

from our resources?

trees like pungan, neem, karanji, ratanjyot or jatropha can be grown to produce 
oil. Athousand such trees can be planted on one hectare, which will yield 10 tonnes 
of oilseeds, from which 2. 5 tonnes of oil can be extracted. This oil can be 
converted into bio diesel after esterification and used as fuel in diesel engines. 
We have the world's largest iivestock population of 250 million, which 
produces close to 125 million tonnes of cow dung. Using this, we can produce 
enough methane gas to entirely replace LPG and kerosene in cooking, and

electricity to meet all requirements at least in rural areas. A developing country like

take to methane farming. He rightly said that methane farming would counter 
the skyrocketing prices of crude oil and merge as an alternative to fossil fuels 
whose stocks may be depleted in t he next 30-40 years. Hence I r equest the 
Government to take rapid and effective measures in this respect.

Concern over unchecked spread of hepatitis-C virus in the 
Country 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA(Himachal Pradesh): Sir, the unchecked spread of 
Hepatitis-C in the country has assumed alarming proportions. It is estimated 
that, in the National Capital Region of Delhi alone, four lakh people are 
suffering from this virus and the number of people afflicted in the country is much 
more. According to experts, the number is rising steadily because of low 
awareness level in non-specific symptoms that make diagnosis difficult and is a 
long drawn process. Hepatitis-C was first detected in 1989, and is relatively a new 
entrant in the epidemiology scene. The virus is blood-borne and is commonly 
transmitted through blood and blood products or through infected syringes. 
There are also instances of transmission from mother to unborn child or through 
sexual intercourse. The rapid spreadi ng of the virus among intravenous drug 
users is another cause of serious concer. 
Sir, Hepatitis-C, unlike most other types of hepatitis, has no relation to water or 
food contamination. Though it has a similar mode of transmission as Hepatitis-B, 
The advent of this dreaded virus has remained largely unchronicled. It is 
shocking that even though this virus has been around for fift een years, the 
awareness levels have remained low and the methods of di agnosis poor and 
inadequate. In view of the near fatal characteristics of this disease, it was 
expected of the health authorities to undertake research for its prevention and 
cure. Also, there is a real need to educate the people especially the vulnerable 
sections of the society to check its spre ad. The Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare needs to take urgent measures to monitor and control the disease.

country 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Kamataka): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, the 
prevailing public contempt for law and the judicial system is aptly echoed in the

sweep and content of Article 21 of the Constitution.

MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Ashwani Kumar. You have five minutes

SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Mr Deputy C hairman, Sir, I don't think it is 
possible for any speaker to do justice to the foreign policy debate when the 
sword of guillotine is hanging over one's head. But I will make only three 
points with no illusion as to the satisfac tion of myself and Members of the 
House that I have done justice to my brief. But let me, in four or five minutes, 
complete what I have to say. 
Sir, we are debating this very impo rtant subject of the nation's foreign 
policy in a particular context. The c ontext is the undisputed emergence of 
India's pre-eminent position in the comity of nations. This pre-eminent position 
of India is as much a product of the way we have pursued our foreign policy, 
the way our diplomacy has conducted itsel f, as it is of our inherent resilence 
as a nation. Foreign policy, in the ultimate analysis, is no more and no less 
than an extension of a nation's national agenda. Therefore, there are three 
non-negotiable principles on which the pursuit of a nation's foreign policy is 
perched, (a) Does it ensure independence of action? (b) Does it subserve the 
non-negotiable interests of a nation? (c) Does it secure the relevance of a 
country in the portals of power, in t he corridors of power in the comity of 
nations? Sir, I beg to state that judged by all these three parameters, India's 
foreign policy has stood the test of time. We continue to remain relevant and 
that is exemplified in the visits that we are now seeing, of President Putin, 
Prime Ministers of Malaysia, Nepal and Pakistan, Foreign Ministers of Japan 
and France. There is no country which is not wishing to engage itself with 
India at the highest levels. That itself shows that th is nation has ensured its 
relevance and our foreign policy is something we must take pride in. 
Sir, the second point which I want to make is this. Are we pursuing our 
national agenda which is non-negotiable? The answer is "yes". While we must 
consolidate our relationship with our trad itional allies, it must not thwart our 
independence of action in engaging with new friends and in soliciting new 
friends. Israel is a case in point. Our relationship with Western Asia must not 
prevent us from pursuing a relationshi p a constructive dialogue, with any 
nation, including Israel. 
Sir, the third point is that foreign po licy is as much a function of a nation's 
soft power as its hard power. We have always, perched our foreign

policy, since the days of Jawaharlal Nehru including Rajiv Gandhi's plan of

pursued the hard power path and that is why we are today a nuclear power. A

Therefore, it is only right to say that the foreign policy is a continuum. It must 
always remain a continuum. That is why it is based on national consensus. That 
is why Foreign Policy is kept above partisan politics and convention was 
breached when the distinguished former Foreign Minister stated in Israel that 
our policy towards Israel was captive to domestic politics. No, Sir. Our foreing 
policy has never been captive to domestic  politics, but it has been captive to 
domestic interest and it will always remain captive to domestic interest, our 
overarching national interests. The distinguished External Affairs Minister is here. 
Nobody is better equipped to project India's foreign policy priorities. I would 
only ask the Minister for Foreign Affairs to take care the following. We need to 
Strengthen the nexus between Russia, China and India just as we continue our 
dialogue with the United States. Our relations with Iran must improve. Sir, our 
neighbours must not live in fear of us. They should respect us. There should be a 
commonality and they should see India as someone who would come to their 
aid in time of need. Increased cooperation with Japan is an absolute 
imperative. This is the Asian Century. I invoke the doctrine of economic power 
as the final testament to our power. In this Asian Century, this decade must 
therefore be a decade of India-Japan axis. Japan is willing and prepared. Prime

visit to India early next year, so has the Chinese Prime Minister who said, "He is 
looking forward to coming to India early next year." Sir, all these indicia 
demonstrate conclusively and decisively that India's foreign policy has delivered. 
Thank you.
